Getting started with BamScaleR

Chirag Parsania

Source: vignettes/BamScaleR-intro.Rmd
BamScaleR-intro.Rmd

Introduction

BamScaleR provides multithreaded sequential BAM traversal for R/Bioconductor workflows. The package is designed for users who already rely on Rsamtools, GenomicAlignments, and BiocParallel, but need faster BAM parsing without moving to a separate non-Bioconductor workflow model.

The package targets four common classes of BAM access:

  • metadata-oriented scans for filtering, fragment summaries, and quality control
  • generation of alignment objects for downstream GenomicAlignments workflows
  • sequence and quality extraction, including an optimized compact mode
  • summaries computed inside the multithreaded reader (fragment-size and mapping-quality distributions, per-base coverage, bigWig tracks), so that no per-read R objects are created at all

The motivation for inclusion in Bioconductor is therefore straightforward: BamScaleR accelerates a core data-access bottleneck while preserving familiar Bioconductor inputs and output types.

BamScaleR is built on the ompBAM C++ library, which supplies parallel BAM decompression. The section BamScaleR and ompBAM below explains what each package provides.

Installation 

if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}

BiocManager::install("BamScaleR")

Multithreading and OpenMP

BamScaleR reads each BAM with several threads (the threads argument) using OpenMP. OpenMP is optional. Without it, every function works and returns the same results, but each BAM is read on a single thread. Processing several files in parallel through BPPARAM (see below) is unaffected. If threads greater than 1 is requested on a build without OpenMP, BamScaleR warns once per session.

  • Linux and Windows. The standard R toolchains (GCC, and Rtools on Windows) support OpenMP. Nothing extra is needed.
  • macOS. Apple’s clang can compile OpenMP code, but Apple does not ship the OpenMP header (omp.h) or runtime library (libomp). CRAN’s R for macOS ships a libomp in R.home("lib"), but no header. When BamScaleR is installed from source, its configure script tries several compiler and linker settings. For each one it builds a small OpenMP test library and loads it into R, and it uses the first setting that loads. With CRAN’s R, the runtime that gets linked is always R’s own libomp, so only one OpenMP runtime is loaded into the R session. The chosen flags are printed in the installation log. If no setting works, the package is built without OpenMP and the log says why. (If your own compiler flags switch OpenMP on for every package, for example CPPFLAGS += -Xclang -fopenmp in ~/.R/Makevars, a build without OpenMP is not possible; configure then stops and says so.)

To enable multithreading on macOS, install the OpenMP files that match your Xcode version from https://mac.r-project.org/openmp/. Check the Apple clang version with clang --version in a terminal. For example, for Xcode 16.0 to 16.2 (Apple clang 1600):

curl -O https://mac.r-project.org/openmp/openmp-17.0.6-darwin20-Release.tar.gz
sudo tar fvxz openmp-17.0.6-darwin20-Release.tar.gz -C /

Use openmp-16.0.4-darwin20-Release.tar.gz for Xcode 15 (Apple clang 1500), or openmp-19.1.5-darwin20-Release.tar.gz for Xcode 16.3 or later (Apple clang 1700). The tarball installs omp.h under /usr/local/include and libomp.dylib under /usr/local/lib. A Homebrew installation (brew install libomp) is also detected.

Then reinstall BamScaleR from source. A plain BiocManager::install() would skip a package that is already installed, or install the same binary again, so ask for a source build explicitly (this needs the Xcode Command Line Tools):

BiocManager::install("BamScaleR", type = "source", force = TRUE)

In a source checkout, rebuild with R CMD INSTALL --preclean . or devtools::load_all(recompile = TRUE), so that objects compiled without OpenMP are not reused.

Apple clang 1700 (Xcode 16.3 and later) needs an OpenMP runtime from LLVM 19 or later. If the libomp bundled with your R is older, configure rejects it, the package is built without OpenMP, and the installation log explains why.

To bypass the detection, set both flags yourself before installing, for example:

Sys.setenv(
    BAMSCALER_OPENMP_CXXFLAGS = "-Xclang -fopenmp",
    BAMSCALER_OPENMP_LIBS = "-lomp"
)
BiocManager::install("BamScaleR", type = "source", force = TRUE)

Setting both variables to "" builds without OpenMP.

Basic usage 

library(BamScaleR)

bam <- ompBAM::example_BAM("Unsorted")

The example file shipped with ompBAM is a small paired-end RNA-seq BAM (10,000 alignments to the human genome, aligned with STAR).

Metadata-oriented BAM access

The most common BAM-access pattern is extraction of alignment metadata such as read name, flag, reference name, position, mapping quality, and CIGAR string.

x <- bam_read(
    file = bam,
    what = c("qname", "flag", "rname", "pos", "mapq", "cigar"),
    as = "data.frame",
    threads = 2
)

head(x)
#>                                       qname flag rname      pos mapq
#> 1  ST-E00600:137:H77Y3CCXY:1:1101:6837:1309  163    19   572614  255

Filtering with ScanBamParam

BamScaleR accepts Rsamtools::ScanBamParam, allowing existing filtering logic to be reused directly.

param <- Rsamtools::ScanBamParam(
    what = c("qname", "flag", "mapq"),
    mapqFilter = 20L,
    flag = Rsamtools::scanBamFlag(isUnmappedQuery = FALSE)
)

filtered <- bam_read(
    file = bam,
    param = param,
    as = "data.frame",
    threads = 2
)

head(filtered)
#>                                       qname flag mapq
#> 1  ST-E00600:137:H77Y3CCXY:1:1101:6837:1309  163  255
#> 2  ST-E00600:137:H77Y3CCXY:1:1101:6837:1309   83  255
#> 3 ST-E00600:137:H77Y3CCXY:1:1101:10450:1309  163  255

#> 6 ST-E00600:137:H77Y3CCXY:1:1101:15077:1309  147  255

Alignment-object output

When downstream workflows expect GenomicAlignments objects, bam_read() can return those directly.

ga <- bam_read(

    what = c("qname", "flag", "rname", "pos", "cigar", "strand"),
    as = "GAlignments",

Sequence and quality extraction

For seq and qual, BamScaleR supports both a compatibility-preserving mode and an optimized compact mode. The compatible mode (the default) returns the sequences and qualities as Biostrings::DNAStringSet and Biostrings::PhredQuality objects, identical to those from Rsamtools::scanBam(). A DataFrame holds such columns naturally; a base data.frame can carry them, but cannot print them.

seqqual_compatible <- bam_read(
    file = bam,
    what = c("qname", "seq", "qual"),
    as = "DataFrame",
    seqqual_mode = "compatible",
    threads = 2
)

seqqual_compatible
#> DataFrame with 10000 rows and 3 columns
#>                        qname                     seq                    qual
#>                  <character>          <DNAStringSet>          <PhredQuality>

#> 2     ST-E00600:137:H77Y3C.. TGCCGGCACA...GCCAGAAAAN -FAAA)-AJF...JJF-AFAAA#

#> 4     ST-E00600:137:H77Y3C.. TGGGAAGAGC...AGATGGTGAN AJA-FFJJJF...JJF<FFAAA#
#> 5     ST-E00600:137:H77Y3C.. NGCATCTCTA...ACATTATTCG #AAFFF-FJJ...JJJJ-<<FJJ
#> ...                      ...                     ...                     ...
#> 9996  ST-E00600:137:H77Y3C.. TTTGATGTTT...GTGCGGTTAT JJA-<FJJJJ...JJJ7JFFF<A

Compact mode returns lower-level raw vectors for throughput-oriented workflows. These values can be decoded back to ordinary strings explicitly when needed.

seqqual_compact <- bam_read(
    file = bam,
    what = c("qname", "qwidth", "seq", "qual"),
    as = "data.frame",
    seqqual_mode = "compact",
    threads = 2
)

head(seqqual_compact)
#>                                       qname qwidth          seq         qual

seqqual_decoded <- decode_seqqual_compact(seqqual_compact)

Fast count summaries

bam_count() provides chromosome-level count summaries using the same BAM filtering model.

counts <- bam_count(bam, threads = 2)

Summaries computed inside the reader

Many analyses do not need the alignments themselves, only a summary of them: a fragment-size distribution for ATAC-seq or ChIP-seq quality control, a mapping-quality profile, or per-base coverage for a genome-browser track. The usual route reads every alignment into R first and then summarises it. The four functions in this section instead compute the summary inside the multithreaded reader. Each thread keeps its own running totals while it decodes its share of the file, and only the finished summary is returned to R. The checks below compare each result with the standard Bioconductor route.

All four functions accept a ScanBamParam, of which the flag and mapqFilter settings are applied to each read. (They cannot restrict the summary to regions, so setting which gives a warning.) The following filter (mapped, primary, passing QC) is the usual one for fragment-size QC:

qc_flag <- Rsamtools::scanBamFlag(
    isUnmappedQuery = FALSE,
    isSecondaryAlignment = FALSE,
    isNotPassingQualityControls = FALSE
)
qc_param <- Rsamtools::ScanBamParam(flag = qc_flag)

Fragment-size distribution: fragment_sizes()

fragment_sizes() tabulates the absolute template length (abs(TLEN), the isize field in Rsamtools) of every read that passes the filter. It returns a data.frame with one row per observed fragment size, in increasing order, and the number of reads with that size. Reads that are unmapped, or whose mate is unmapped, have no defined fragment size and are excluded by default (drop_mate_unmapped = TRUE), just as scanBam() reports NA for them.

fs <- fragment_sizes(bam, param = qc_param, threads = 2)
str(fs)
#> 'data.frame':    2047 obs. of  2 variables:
#>  $ fragment_size: int  59 76 78 79 84 85 86 89 91 93 ...
#>  $ count        : num  2 2 2 2 4 2 2 4 4 2 ...

## the most common fragment size
fs[which.max(fs$count), ]
#>     fragment_size count
#> 122           212    62
short <- fs[fs$fragment_size <= 1000, ]
plot(short$fragment_size, short$count, type = "h",
     xlab = "Fragment size (bp)", ylab = "Reads")

Fragment-size distribution of the example BAM (fragments up to 1 kb).

The same table computed the standard way, by reading every isize into R and tabulating it, is identical:

isize <- Rsamtools::scanBam(
    bam,
    param = Rsamtools::ScanBamParam(what = "isize", flag = qc_flag)
)[[1]]$isize
tab <- table(abs(isize))
ref <- data.frame(fragment_size = as.integer(names(tab)),
                  count = as.numeric(tab))
identical(fs, ref)
#> [1] TRUE

Mapping-quality distribution: mapq_dist()

mapq_dist() returns the number of reads at each mapping quality (MAPQ, 0 to 255) as a data.frame with columns mapq and count. Unmapped reads have no mapping quality (scanBam() reports NA for them) and are not counted.

mq <- mapq_dist(bam, param = qc_param, threads = 2)
mq
#>   mapq count
#> 1  255 10000

It is identical to tabulating the mapq values read with scanBam():

mapq <- Rsamtools::scanBam(
    bam,
    param = Rsamtools::ScanBamParam(what = "mapq", flag = qc_flag)
)[[1]]$mapq
tab <- table(mapq)
identical(mq, data.frame(mapq = as.integer(names(tab)),
                         count = as.numeric(tab)))
#> [1] TRUE

The example BAM was aligned with STAR, which gives every uniquely mapped read a MAPQ of 255, so the distribution has a single value. On a BAM from an aligner such as Bowtie 2 or BWA, the table shows the full spread of MAPQ values, and setting mapqFilter in param removes reads below that value from the distribution.

Per-base coverage: bam_coverage()

bam_coverage() returns per-base read depth as an RleList: one run-length encoded integer vector per sequence in the BAM header, in header order, each as long as the sequence. Sequences with no reads are a single run of zeros. CIGAR operations are counted in the same way as GenomicAlignments::coverage(): M, =, X and D add depth, N (a splice junction) does not, and I, S, H and P are ignored.

cov <- bam_coverage(bam, threads = 2)
cov[c("1", "MT")]
#> RleList of length 2
#> $`1`
#> integer-Rle of length 248956422 with 3132 runs
#>   Lengths:  630211      19       4       4 ...      26     123      26 1857649
#>   Values :       0       1       2       3 ...       1       2       1       0
#> 
#> $MT
#> integer-Rle of length 16569 with 518 runs
#>   Lengths: 140   6  24  34  44  42   4  19 ...  32  41  82 520 127  19 131 684
#>   Values :   0   1   2   4   5   6   5   4 ...   1   2   1   0   1   2   1   0

The result is an ordinary RleList, so the usual IRanges tools apply, for example per-chromosome summaries or the regions above a depth threshold:

head(data.frame(
    seqname = names(cov),
    covered_bp = sum(cov > 0),
    max_depth = max(cov)
))
#>    seqname covered_bp max_depth
#> 1        1     108800        21
#> 10      10      28831        10
#> 11      11      52762         9
#> 12      12      52669        12
#> 13      13      15105        11
#> 14      14      20147        13

## regions of the mitochondrial genome covered by at least 10 reads
IRanges::slice(cov[["MT"]], lower = 10)
#> Views on a 16569-length Rle subject
#> 
#> views:
#>      start  end width
#>  [1]  2502 2597    96 [12 12 12 13 13 13 13 13 13 13 13 13 13 13 12 12 12 ...]
#>  [2]  6909 6988    80 [10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 11 11 11 11 11 11 11 11 11 ...]
#>  [3]  7046 7048     3 [10 10 10]
#>  [4]  7107 7124    18 [10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 ...]
#>  [5]  7158 7277   120 [10 10 10 10 10 10 11 11 11 11 11 11 12 12 12 12 12 ...]
#>  [6]  7301 7313    13 [10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10]
#>  [7]  7345 7352     8 [10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10]
#>  [8]  7819 7829    11 [10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10]
#>  [9]  8095 8115    21 [10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 ...]
#> [10]  8146 8203    58 [10 11 11 11 11 11 11 11 11 11 11 11 11 11 11 11 11 ...]
#> [11]  9766 9820    55 [10 10 10 10 10 10 11 11 11 11 11 11 11 11 10 10 10 ...]
#> [12]  9826 9932   107 [10 10 10 10 10 10 11 11 11 11 13 13 13 13 13 13 13 ...]

It is identical to the coverage computed from a GAlignments object:

ref_cov <- GenomicAlignments::coverage(
    GenomicAlignments::readGAlignments(bam)
)
identical(cov, ref_cov)
#> [1] TRUE

Coverage straight to a bigWig file: bam_coverage_bigwig()

To make a genome-browser track, bam_coverage_bigwig() computes the same coverage and writes it directly to a bigWig file, without creating the coverage RleList in R. It returns the path of the file it wrote (invisibly). Only non-zero runs are written, which is the bigWig convention; uncovered bases read back as zero.

bw <- tempfile(fileext = ".bw")
bam_coverage_bigwig(bam, outfile = bw, threads = 2)
file.size(bw)
#> [1] 271289

The file can be loaded into a genome browser or read back into R with rtracklayer. The values match bam_coverage() on every sequence (a bigWig stores them as floating-point numbers, so they are compared as numbers):

imported <- rtracklayer::import(bw, as = "RleList")
all(vapply(names(cov), function(chr) {
    isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(imported[[chr]]), as.numeric(cov[[chr]])))
}, logical(1)))
#> [1] TRUE

Several files at once

Every function accepts several BAM files, as a character vector or an Rsamtools::BamFileList, and returns a named list with one result per file. Files are processed in parallel according to BPPARAM, and threads sets the number of threads used within each file. The BPPARAM object is used as supplied and is not modified, so it can be reused for other work afterwards. (On Linux, GCC’s OpenMP runtime cannot start threads in a forked MulticoreParam worker once the R session has used OpenMP threads, and the worker would wait forever. BamScaleR releases the runtime’s idle threads before each fork(), so forked workers use threads as requested. This needs libgomp 9 or later; with an older runtime, use SnowParam() instead.)

two <- fragment_sizes(
    c(rep1 = bam, rep2 = bam),
    param = qc_param,
    threads = 1,
    BPPARAM = BiocParallel::SerialParam()
)
vapply(two, function(x) sum(x$count), numeric(1))
#>  rep1  rep2 
#> 10000 10000

Relationship to existing Bioconductor tools

BamScaleR is intended to complement, not replace, existing Bioconductor packages.

  • Rsamtools remains the canonical low-level BAM access layer in R and defines the filtering idioms that BamScaleR reuses through ScanBamParam.
  • GenomicAlignments remains the standard package for alignment-centric downstream workflows, and BamScaleR supports direct generation of compatible alignment objects.
  • BiocParallel remains the standard mechanism for file-level parallelism, and BamScaleR adds a second axis of parallelism through per-file OpenMP threads.

The main difference is therefore performance-oriented: BamScaleR accelerates the traversal step itself while staying close to existing Bioconductor usage patterns.

BamScaleR and ompBAM

ompBAM and BamScaleR work at different levels.

ompBAM is a header-only C++ library for package developers. It opens a BAM file, decompresses its compressed (BGZF) blocks on several OpenMP threads, and gives each thread a share of the raw alignment records, with C++ functions to read the fields of one record (flag, position, CIGAR, tags and so on). It has no R function that reads a BAM file into R; its R functions are helpers for developers, such as use_ompBAM() and example_BAM(). To do anything with the records, a package must write its own C++ loop over them.

BamScaleR is that loop, together with what is needed to use its output in Bioconductor workflows:

  • R functions with Rsamtools semantics. bam_read() takes the what fields of Rsamtools::scanBam() (except groupid and mate_status), its tag fields and ScanBamParam settings (flag, mapqFilter, which), and applies them to each record in C++. (which selects the alignments that overlap a range, as in Rsamtools; ?bam_read lists the remaining differences.) bam_count() and the summary functions apply the filters listed on their help pages, and warn about settings they cannot apply.
  • Bioconductor output objects. Results from all threads are merged in file order and converted into a data.frame or DataFrame, a scanBam()-style list (with DNAStringSet and PhredQuality for sequences and qualities), a GAlignments or a GAlignmentPairs object; the columns and the GAlignments slots are built in compiled code. The package tests compare fields, sequences and qualities with Rsamtools::scanBam(), and GAlignments objects with readGAlignments(), using identical(). They also check that, without which, GAlignmentPairs output contains the same pairs as readGAlignmentPairs(), including for secondary and supplementary alignments.
  • Summaries inside the reader. Per-chromosome counts, fragment-size and mapping-quality distributions, per-base coverage, and a bigWig writer (a bundled copy of libBigWig, extended to compress blocks in parallel).
  • Two levels of parallelism. OpenMP threads within a file and BiocParallel workers across files. With auto_threads = TRUE the two are balanced against the number of available cores.
  • Portable builds. The configure script described under Installation finds a working OpenMP setup on macOS.
